Ancient <color=#3366CC>polytheistic</color> religions, such as those of Greece, <color=#3366CC>Rome</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Scandinavia</color>, are usually categorized under the
heading of <color=#3366CC>mythology</color>. Religions of pre-industrial peoples, or <color=#3366CC>cultures</color> in development, are similarly called myths in the
<color=#3366CC>anthropology of religion</color>. The term myth can be used pejoratively by both religious and non-religious people. By defining
another person's religious stories and beliefs as mythology, one implies that they are less real or true than one's own
religious stories and beliefs. <color=#3366CC>Joseph Campbell</color> remarked, "Mythology is often thought of as other people's religions, and
religion can be defined as misinterpreted mythology."
In sociology, however, the term myth has a non-pejorative meaning. There, myth is defined as a story that is important
for the group, whether or not it is objectively or provably true. Examples include the <color=#3366CC>resurrection</color> of their real-life founder
<color=#3366CC>Jesus</color>, which, to Christians, explains the means by which they are freed from sin, is symbolic of the power of life over
death, and is also said to be a historical event. But from a mythological outlook, whether or not the event actually
occurred is unimportant. Instead, the <color=#3366CC>symbolism</color> of the death of an old life and the start of a new life is most significant.
Religious believers may or may not accept such symbolic interpretations.
Practices

The practices of a religion may include <color=#3366CC>rituals</color>, <color=#3366CC>sermons</color>, commemoration or veneration of a <color=#3366CC>deity</color> (god or <color=#3366CC>goddess</color>),

<color=#3366CC>sacrifices</color>, <color=#3366CC>festivals</color>, <color=#3366CC>feasts</color>, <color=#3366CC>trances</color>, initiations, <color=#3366CC>funerary services</color>, <color=#3366CC>matrimonial services</color>, <color=#3366CC>meditation</color>, <color=#3366CC>prayer</color>, <color=#3366CC>religious</color>
<color=#3366CC>music</color>, <color=#3366CC>religious art</color>, <color=#3366CC>sacred dance</color>, public service, or other aspects of human culture. Barriers to exit a religion vary,
ranging from <color=#3366CC>freedom of religion</color> to death for <color=#3366CC>apostasy</color>, which can result in <color=#3366CC>coercion</color> through <color=#3366CC>deterrence</color>.
Social organisation
Religions have a societal basis, either as a living tradition which is carried by lay participants, or with an organized
<color=#3366CC>clergy</color>, and a definition of what constitutes adherence or membership.
Academic study
A number of disciplines study the phenomenon of religion: <color=#3366CC>theology</color>, <color=#3366CC>comparative religion</color>, <color=#3366CC>history of religion</color>,
<color=#3366CC>evolutionary origin of religions</color>, <color=#3366CC>anthropology of religion</color>, <color=#3366CC>psychology of religion</color> (including neuroscience of religion and
evolutionary psychology of religion), law and religion, and sociology of religion.
Daniel L. Pals mentions eight classical theories of religion, focusing on various aspects of religion: <color=#3366CC>animism</color> and <color=#3366CC>magic</color>,

by <color=#3366CC>E.B. Tylor</color> and <color=#3366CC>J.G. Frazer</color>; the <color=#3366CC>psycho-analytic</color> approach of <color=#3366CC>Sigmund Freud</color>; and further <color=#3366CC>Émile Durkheim</color>, <color=#3366CC>Karl Marx</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Max Weber</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mircea Eliade</color>, <color=#3366CC>E.E. Evans-Pritchard</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Clifford Geertz</color>.
Michael Stausberg gives an overview of contemporary theories of religion, including cognitive and biological
approaches.
Theories
Sociological and <color=#3366CC>anthropological</color> theories of religion generally attempt to explain the <color=#3366CC>origin</color> and <color=#3366CC>function of religion</color>.
These theories define what they present as universal characteristics of <color=#3366CC>religious belief</color> and practice.
Origins and development
The origin of religion is uncertain. There are a number of theories regarding the subsequent origins of religious
practices.
According to anthropologists John Monaghan and Peter Just, "Many of the great world religions appear to have begun
as revitalization movements of some sort, as the vision of a charismatic prophet fires the imaginations of people
seeking a more comprehensive answer to their problems than they feel is provided by everyday beliefs. Charismatic
individuals have emerged at many times and places in the world. It seems that the key to long-term success—and
many movements come and go with little long-term effect—has relatively little to do with the prophets, who appear with
surprising regularity, but more to do with the development of a group of supporters who are able to institutionalize the
movement."
The <color=#3366CC>development of religion</color> has taken different forms in different cultures. Some religions place an emphasis on belief,
while others emphasize practice. Some religions focus on the subjective experience of the religious individual, while
others consider the activities of the religious community to be most important. Some religions claim to be universal,
believing their <color=#3366CC>laws</color> and <color=#3366CC>cosmology</color> to be binding for everyone, while others are intended to be practiced only by a
closely defined or localized group. In many places, religion has been associated with public institutions such as
<color=#3366CC>education</color>, <color=#3366CC>hospitals</color>, the <color=#3366CC>family</color>, <color=#3366CC>government</color>, and <color=#3366CC>political</color> hierarchies.
Anthropologists John Monoghan and Peter Just state that, "it seems apparent that one thing religion or belief helps us
do is deal with problems of human life that are significant, persistent, and intolerable. One important way in which
religious beliefs accomplish this is by providing a set of ideas about how and why the world is put together that allows
people to accommodate anxieties and deal with misfortune."
Cultural system
While religion is difficult to define, one standard model of religion, used in <color=#3366CC>religious studies</color> courses, was proposed by
<color=#3366CC>Clifford Geertz</color>, who simply called it a "cultural system". A critique of Geertz's model by Talal Asad categorized religion
as "an <color=#3366CC>anthropological</color> category". Richard Niebuhr's (1894–1962) five-fold classification of the relationship between
Christ and culture, however, indicates that religion and culture can be seen as two separate systems, though with some
interplay.
Social constructionism
One modern academic theory of religion, <color=#3366CC>social constructionism</color>, says that religion is a modern concept that suggests
all <color=#3366CC>spiritual</color> practice and <color=#3366CC>worship</color> follows a model similar to the <color=#3366CC>Abrahamic religions</color> as an orientation system that helps
to interpret reality and define human beings. Among the main proponents of this theory of religion are Daniel
Dubuisson, Timothy Fitzgerald, Talal Asad, and Jason Ānanda Josephson. The social constructionists argue that
religion is a modern concept that developed from Christianity and was then applied inappropriately to non-Western
cultures.
Cognitive science
Cognitive science of religion is the study of religious thought and behavior from the perspective of the cognitive and
evolutionary sciences. The field employs methods and theories from a very broad range of disciplines, including:
<color=#3366CC>cognitive psychology</color>, <color=#3366CC>evolutionary psychology</color>, cognitive anthropology, <color=#3366CC>artificial intelligence</color>, cognitive neuroscience,
<color=#3366CC>neurobiology</color>, <color=#3366CC>zoology</color>, and <color=#3366CC>ethology</color>. Scholars in this field seek to explain how human minds acquire, generate, and
transmit religious thoughts, practices, and schemas by means of ordinary cognitive capacities.
<color=#3366CC>Hallucinations</color> and delusions related to religious content occurs in about 60% of people with <color=#3366CC>schizophrenia</color>. While this
number varies across cultures, this had led to theories about a number of influential religious phenomena and possible
relation to psychotic disorders. A number of prophetic experiences are consistent with psychotic symptoms, although
retrospective diagnoses are practically impossible. Schizophrenic episodes are also experienced by people who do not
have belief in gods.
Religious content is also common in temporal lobe epilepsy, and <color=#3366CC>obsessive-compulsive disorder</color>. Atheistic content is
also found to be common with temporal lobe epilepsy.
Comparativism
Comparative religion is the branch of the <color=#3366CC>study of religions</color> concerned with the systematic comparison of the doctrines
and practices of the world's religions. In general, the comparative study of religion yields a deeper understanding of the
fundamental philosophical concerns of religion such as <color=#3366CC>ethics</color>, <color=#3366CC>metaphysics</color>, and the nature and form of <color=#3366CC>salvation</color>.
Studying such material is meant to give one a richer and more sophisticated understanding of human beliefs and
practices regarding the <color=#3366CC>sacred</color>, numinous, <color=#3366CC>spiritual</color> and <color=#3366CC>divine</color>.
In the field of comparative religion, a common geographical classification of the main world religions includes Middle
Eastern religions (including <color=#3366CC>Zoroastrianism</color> and Iranian religions), <color=#3366CC>Indian religions</color>, East Asian religions, African
religions, American religions, Oceanic religions, and classical Hellenistic religions.
Classification
In the 19th and 20th centuries, the academic practice of <color=#3366CC>comparative religion</color> divided religious belief into philosophically
defined categories called world religions. Some academics <color=#3366CC>studying the subject</color> have divided religions into three broad
categories:
• World religions, a term which refers to transcultural, international religions;
• Indigenous religions, which refers to smaller, culture-specific or nation-specific religious groups; and
• <color=#3366CC>New religious movements</color>, which refers to recently developed religions.
Some recent scholarship has argued that not all types of religion are necessarily separated by mutually exclusive
philosophies, and furthermore that the utility of ascribing a practice to a certain philosophy, or even calling a given
practice religious, rather than cultural, political, or social in nature, is limited. The current state of psychological study
about the nature of religiousness suggests that it is better to refer to religion as a largely invariant phenomenon that
should be distinguished from cultural norms (i.e. religions).
Morphological classification
Some <color=#3366CC>religion scholars</color> classify religions as either universal religions that seek worldwide acceptance and actively look
for new <color=#3366CC>converts</color>, such as the Baháí Faith, Buddhism, Christianity, Islam, and Jainism, while <color=#3366CC>ethnic religions</color> are
identified with a particular ethnic group and do not seek converts. Others reject the distinction, saying that all religious
practices, whatever their philosophical origin, are ethnic because they come from a particular culture.
Demographic classification
The four largest religious groups by world population, estimated to account for 5.8 billion people and 73% of the
population, are Christianity, Islam, Buddhism and Hinduism (with the relative numbers for Buddhism and Hinduism
dependent on the extent of <color=#3366CC>syncretism</color>).
A global poll in 2012 surveyed 57 countries and reported that 59% of the world's population identified as religious, 23%
as <color=#3366CC>not religious</color>, 13% as convinced <color=#3366CC>atheists</color>, and also a 9% decrease in identification as religious when compared to the
2005 average from 39 countries. A follow-up poll in 2015 found that 63% of the globe identified as religious, 22% as not
religious, and 11% as convinced atheists. On average, women are more religious than men. Some people follow
multiple religions or multiple religious principles at the same time, regardless of whether or not the religious principles
they follow traditionally allow for <color=#3366CC>syncretism</color>. Unaffiliated populations are projected to drop, even when taking
disaffiliation rates into account, due to differences in birth rates.
Scholars have indicated that global religiosity may be increasing due to religious countries having higher birth rates in
general.
Specific religions
Abrahamic
<color=#3366CC>Abrahamic religions</color> are <color=#3366CC>monotheistic</color> religions which believe they descend from <color=#3366CC>Abraham</color>.
Judaism
<color=#3366CC>Judaism</color> is the oldest Abrahamic religion, originating in the people of <color=#3366CC>ancient Israel and Judah</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Torah</color> is its
foundational text, and is part of the larger text known as the <color=#3366CC>Tanakh</color> or <color=#3366CC>Hebrew Bible</color>. It is supplemented by oral
tradition, set down in written form in later texts such as the <color=#3366CC>Midrash</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Talmud</color>. Judaism includes a wide corpus of
texts, practices, theological positions, and forms of organization. Within Judaism there are a variety of movements,
most of which emerged from <color=#3366CC>Rabbinic Judaism</color>, which holds that God revealed his laws and commandments to <color=#3366CC>Moses</color>
on Mount Sinai in the form of both the <color=#3366CC>Written</color> and <color=#3366CC>Oral Torah</color>; historically, this assertion was challenged by various
groups. The <color=#3366CC>Jewish people</color> were scattered after the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem in 70 CE. Today there are
about 13 million Jews, about 40 per cent living in Israel and 40 per cent in the United States. The largest <color=#3366CC>Jewish</color>
<color=#3366CC>religious movements</color> are <color=#3366CC>Orthodox Judaism</color> (<color=#3366CC>Haredi Judaism</color> and Modern Orthodox Judaism), <color=#3366CC>Conservative Judaism</color>
and <color=#3366CC>Reform Judaism</color>.
Christianity
<color=#3366CC>Christianity</color> is based on the life and teachings of <color=#3366CC>Jesus</color> of Nazareth (1st century) as presented in the New Testament.
The Christian faith is essentially faith in Jesus as the <color=#3366CC>Christ</color>, the Son of God, and as <color=#3366CC>Savior</color> and Lord. Almost all

Christians believe in the <color=#3366CC>Trinity</color>, which teaches the unity of <color=#3366CC>Father</color>, <color=#3366CC>Son</color> (Jesus Christ), and <color=#3366CC>Holy Spirit</color> as three persons
in one Godhead. Most Christians can describe their faith with the <color=#3366CC>Nicene Creed</color>. As the religion of <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color> in
the first millennium and of <color=#3366CC>Western Europe</color> during the time of colonization, Christianity has been propagated throughout
the world via <color=#3366CC>missionary work</color>. It is the world's largest religion, with about 2.3 billion followers as of 2015. The main
divisions of Christianity are, according to the number of adherents:
• The <color=#3366CC>Catholic Church</color>, led by the <color=#3366CC>Bishop of Rome</color> and the bishops worldwide in communion with him, is a
communion of 24 Churches sui iuris, including the Latin Church and 23 <color=#3366CC>Eastern Catholic churches</color>, such as the
Maronite Catholic Church.
• <color=#3366CC>Eastern Christianity</color>, which include <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodoxy</color>, <color=#3366CC>Oriental Orthodoxy</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Church of the East</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Protestantism</color>, separated from the Catholic Church in the 16th-century <color=#3366CC>Protestant Reformation</color> and is split into
thousands of <color=#3366CC>denominations</color>. Major branches of Protestantism include <color=#3366CC>Anglicanism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Baptists</color>, <color=#3366CC>Calvinism</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Lutheranism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Methodism</color>, though each of these contain many different denominations or groups.
There are also smaller groups, including:
• <color=#3366CC>Restorationism</color>, the belief that Christianity should be restored (as opposed to reformed) along the lines of what is
known about the apostolic early church.
• Latter-day Saint movement, founded by <color=#3366CC>Joseph Smith</color> in the late 1820s.
• <color=#3366CC>Jehovah's Witnesses</color>, founded in the late 1870s by <color=#3366CC>Charles Taze Russell</color>.
Islam

<color=#3366CC>Islam</color> is a <color=#3366CC>monotheistic</color> religion based on the <color=#3366CC>Quran</color>, one of the <color=#3366CC>holy books</color> considered by Muslims to be revealed by
God, and on the <color=#3366CC>teachings (hadith)</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Islamic prophet</color> <color=#3366CC>Muhammad</color>, a major political and religious figure of the 7th
century CE. Islam is based on the unity of all religious philosophies and accepts all of the <color=#3366CC>Abrahamic</color> prophets of
Judaism, Christianity and other Abrahamic religions before <color=#3366CC>Muhammad</color>. It is the most widely practiced religion of

<color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>North Africa</color>, <color=#3366CC>Western Asia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color>, while <color=#3366CC>Muslim-majority countries</color> also exist in parts of
<color=#3366CC>South Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sub-Saharan Africa</color>, and Southeast Europe. There are also several Islamic republics, including <color=#3366CC>Iran</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mauritania</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color>. With about 2 billion followers (2020), a quarter of <color=#3366CC>earth's population</color> are
<color=#3366CC>Muslims</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Sunni Islam</color> is the largest denomination within Islam and follows the Qur'an, the ahadith (plural of Hadith) which
record the <color=#3366CC>sunnah</color>, whilst placing emphasis on the <color=#3366CC>sahabah</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Shia Islam</color> is the second largest denomination of Islam and its adherents believe that <color=#3366CC>Ali</color> succeeded Muhammad
and further places emphasis on Muhammad's family.
• There are also Muslim revivalist movements such as Muwahhidism and <color=#3366CC>Salafism</color>.
Other denominations of Islam include <color=#3366CC>Nation of Islam</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ibadi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sufism</color>, Quranism, Mahdavia, <color=#3366CC>Ahmadiyya</color> and
non-denominational Muslims. <color=#3366CC>Wahhabism</color> is the dominant Muslim <color=#3366CC>schools of thought</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Saudi Arabia</color>.
Other
Judaism, Christianity, and Islam are the three most popular Abrahamic faiths, however there are smaller and newer
traditions that lay claim to the designation of Abrahamic as well.
For example, the <color=#3366CC>Baháí Faith</color>, though often called a <color=#3366CC>new religious movement</color>, claims to be a world religion from the line
of major Abrahamic religions, while recognizing the Indo-Iranian traditions (Hinduism, Buddhism, Zoroastrianism).
Founded in 19th-century Iran, it teaches the unity of all great religious traditions as the progressive unfolding of one
religion and accepts all of the prophets of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam as well as additional prophets (Krishna,
Buddha, Zoroaster), including its founder <color=#3366CC>Bahá'u'lláh</color>. Its initial phase as Bábism forms an integral part of its history.
Even smaller regional Abrahamic groups also exist, including Samaritanism (primarily in Israel and the <color=#3366CC>State of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Palestine</color>), the <color=#3366CC>Rastafari movement</color> (primarily in Jamaica), and <color=#3366CC>Druze</color> (primarily in Syria, Lebanon, and Israel).
The Druze faith originally developed out of <color=#3366CC>Isma'ilism</color>, and it has sometimes been considered an <color=#3366CC>Islamic school</color> by
some Islamic authorities, but Druze themselves do not identify as <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color>. Scholars classify the Druze faith as an
independent Abrahamic religion because it developed its own unique doctrines and eventually separated from both
Isma'ilism and Islam altogether. One of these doctrines includes the belief that <color=#3366CC>Al-Hākim bi-Amr Allāh</color> was an
<color=#3366CC>incarnation of God</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Mandaeism</color>, sometimes also known as Sabianism (after the mysterious Sabians mentioned in the Quran, a name
historically claimed by several religious groups), is a <color=#3366CC>Gnostic</color>, <color=#3366CC>monotheistic</color> and <color=#3366CC>ethnic religion</color>. Its adherents, the
Mandaeans, consider <color=#3366CC>John the Baptist</color> to be their chief prophet. Mandaeans are the last surviving Gnostics from
antiquity.
East Asian
East Asian religions (also known as Far Eastern religions or Taoic religions) consist of several religions of East Asia
which make use of the concept of Tao (in Chinese), Dō (in Japanese or Korean) or Đao (in Vietnamese). They include:
Taoism and Confucianism
• <color=#3366CC>Taoism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Confucianism</color>, as well as Korean, Vietnamese, and Japanese religion influenced by Chinese thought.
Folk religions
<color=#3366CC>Chinese folk religion</color>: the indigenous religions of the <color=#3366CC>Han Chinese</color>, or, by <color=#3366CC>metonymy</color>, of all the populations of the

<color=#3366CC>Chinese cultural sphere</color>. It includes the syncretism of <color=#3366CC>Confucianism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Taoism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>, Wuism, as well as many
new religious movements such as Chen Tao, <color=#3366CC>Falun Gong</color> and Yiguandao.
Other folk and new religions of <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color> such as <color=#3366CC>Korean shamanism</color>, Chondogyo, and Jeung San
Do in Korea; indigenous Philippine folk religions in the <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color>; <color=#3366CC>Shinto</color>, Shugendo, Ryukyuan religion, and Japanese
new religions in Japan; Satsana Phi in Laos; Vietnamese folk religion, and <color=#3366CC>Cao Đài</color>, Hòa Hao in Vietnam.
Indian religions
<color=#3366CC>Indian religions</color> are practiced or were founded in the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color>. They are sometimes classified as the dharmic
religions, as they all feature <color=#3366CC>dharma</color>, the specific law of reality and duties expected according to the religion.
Hinduism
<color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color> is also called Vaidika Dharma, the <color=#3366CC>dharma</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Vedas</color>, although many practitioners refer to their religion as
Sanātana Dharma ("the Eternal Dharma") which refers to the idea that its origins lie beyond <color=#3366CC>human history</color>. Vaidika
Dharma is a synecdoche describing the similar philosophies of <color=#3366CC>Vaishnavism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Shaivism</color>, and related groups practiced or

founded in the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color>. Concepts most of them share in common include <color=#3366CC>karma</color>, <color=#3366CC>caste</color>, <color=#3366CC>reincarnation</color>,
<color=#3366CC>mantras</color>, yantras, and darśana. Deities in Hinduism are referred to as Deva (masculine) and Devi (feminine). Major

deities include <color=#3366CC>Vishnu</color>, <color=#3366CC>Lakshmi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Shiva</color>, <color=#3366CC>Parvati</color>, <color=#3366CC>Brahma</color> and <color=#3366CC>Saraswati</color>. These deities have distinct and complex
personalities yet are often viewed as aspects of the same Ultimate Reality called <color=#3366CC>Brahman</color>. Hinduism is one of the most
ancient of still-active religious belief systems, with origins perhaps as far back as prehistoric times. Therefore, Hinduism
has been called the oldest religion in the world.
Jainism
<color=#3366CC>Jainism</color>, taught primarily by <color=#3366CC>Rishabhanatha</color> (the founder of <color=#3366CC>ahimsa</color>) is an ancient Indian religion that prescribes a path
of <color=#3366CC>non-violence</color>, <color=#3366CC>truth</color> and anekantavada for all forms of living beings in this universe; which helps them to eliminate all
the Karmas, and hence to attain freedom from the cycle of birth and death (samsāra), that is, achieving nirvana. Jains
are found mostly in India. According to Dundas, outside of the Jain tradition, historians date the <color=#3366CC>Mahavira</color> as about
contemporaneous with the <color=#3366CC>Buddha</color> in the 5th-century BCE, and accordingly the historical <color=#3366CC>Parshvanatha</color>, based on the
c. 250-year gap, is placed in 8th or 7th century BCE.
• <color=#3366CC>Digambara</color> Jainism (or sky-clad) is mainly practiced in South India. Their holy books are Pravachanasara and
Samayasara written by their Prophets <color=#3366CC>Kundakunda</color> and Amritchandra as their original canon is lost.
• <color=#3366CC>Shwetambara</color> Jainism (or white-clad) is mainly practiced in Western India. Their holy books are Jain Agamas,
written by their Prophet Sthulibhadra.
Buddhism
<color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color> was founded by <color=#3366CC>Siddhartha Gautama</color> in the 5th century BCE. Buddhists generally agree that Gotama aimed
to help sentient beings end their <color=#3366CC>suffering (dukkha)</color> by understanding the <color=#3366CC>true nature of phenomena</color>, thereby escaping
the cycle of suffering and rebirth (samsāra), that is, achieving nirvana.
• <color=#3366CC>Theravada</color> Buddhism, which is practiced mainly in <color=#3366CC>Sri Lanka</color> and Southeast Asia alongside folk religion, shares
some characteristics of Indian religions. It is based in a large collection of texts called the <color=#3366CC>Pali Canon</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Mahayana</color> Buddhism (or the Great Vehicle) under which are a multitude of doctrines that became prominent in
China and are still relevant in Vietnam, Korea, Japan and to a lesser extent <color=#3366CC>in Europe and the United States</color>.
Mahayana Buddhism includes such disparate teachings as <color=#3366CC>Zen</color> or <color=#3366CC>Pure Land</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Vajrayana</color> Buddhism first appeared in India in the 3rd century CE. It is currently most prominent in the Himalaya
regions and extends across all of Asia (cf. Mikkyō).
• Two notable new Buddhist sects are Hòa Hao and the Navayana (Dalit Buddhist movement), which were
developed separately in the 20th century.
Sikhism
<color=#3366CC>Sikhism</color> is a <color=#3366CC>panentheistic</color> religion founded on the teachings of <color=#3366CC>Guru Nanak</color> and ten successive <color=#3366CC>Sikh gurus</color> in
15th-century <color=#3366CC>Punjab</color>. It is the fifth-largest organized religion in the world, with approximately 30 million Sikhs. Sikhs are
expected to embody the qualities of a Sant-Sipāhī—a saint-soldier, have control over one's internal vices and be able
to be constantly immersed in virtues clarified in the <color=#3366CC>Guru Granth Sahib</color>. The principal beliefs of Sikhi are faith in
Waheguru—represented by the phrase ik ōankār, one cosmic divine actioner (God), who prevails in everything, along
with a praxis in which the Sikh is enjoined to engage in social reform through the pursuit of justice for all human beings.
Indigenous and folk
Indigenous religions or <color=#3366CC>folk religions</color> refers to a broad category of traditional religions that can be characterised by
<color=#3366CC>shamanism</color>, <color=#3366CC>animism</color> and ancestor worship, where traditional means "indigenous, that which is aboriginal or
foundational, handed down from generation to generation...". These are religions that are closely associated with a
particular group of people, ethnicity or tribe; they often have no formal creeds or sacred texts. Some religions are
<color=#3366CC>syncretic</color>, fusing diverse religious beliefs and practices.
• <color=#3366CC>Australian Aboriginal religions</color>.
• Folk religions of the Americas: <color=#3366CC>Native American religions</color>
Folk religions are often omitted as a category in surveys even in countries where they are widely practiced, e.g., in
China.
Traditional African
<color=#3366CC>African traditional religion</color> encompasses the traditional religious beliefs of people in Africa. In West Africa, these
religions include the Akan religion, Dahomey (Fon) mythology, Efik mythology, <color=#3366CC>Odinani</color>, Serer religion (A at Roog), and
<color=#3366CC>Yoruba religion</color>, while Bushongo mythology, Mbuti (Pygmy) mythology, Lugbara mythology, Dinka religion, and Lotuko
mythology come from central Africa. Southern African traditions include Akamba mythology, Masai mythology,
Malagasy mythology, San religion, Lozi mythology, Tumbuka mythology, and Zulu mythology. <color=#3366CC>Bantu mythology</color> is found
throughout central, southeast, and southern Africa. In north Africa, these traditions include Berber and <color=#3366CC>ancient</color>
<color=#3366CC>Egyptian</color>.
There are also notable African diasporic religions practiced in the Americas, such as <color=#3366CC>Santeria</color>, <color=#3366CC>Candomble</color>, <color=#3366CC>Vodun</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Lucumi</color>, Umbanda, and Macumba.
Iranian
Iranian religions are ancient religions whose roots predate the Islamization of <color=#3366CC>Greater Iran</color>. Nowadays these religions
are practiced only by minorities.
<color=#3366CC>Zoroastrianism</color> is based on the teachings of prophet <color=#3366CC>Zoroaster</color> in the 6th century BCE. Zoroastrians worship the <color=#3366CC>creator</color>
<color=#3366CC>Ahura Mazda</color>. In Zoroastrianism, good and evil have distinct sources, with evil trying to destroy the creation of Mazda,
and good trying to sustain it.
Kurdish religions include the traditional beliefs of the Yazidi, <color=#3366CC>Alevi</color>, and Ahl-e Haqq. Sometimes these are labeled
Yazdânism.
New religious movements
• The <color=#3366CC>Baháí Faith</color> teaches the unity of all religions.
• <color=#3366CC>Cao Đài</color> is a <color=#3366CC>syncretistic</color>, <color=#3366CC>monotheistic</color> religion, established in <color=#3366CC>Vietnam</color> in 1926.
• Eckankar is a <color=#3366CC>pantheistic</color> religion with the purpose of making God an everyday reality in one's life.
• Epicureanism is a Hellenistic philosophy that is considered by many of its practitioners as a type of (sometimes
non-theistic) religious identity. It has its own scriptures, a monthly "feast of reason" on the Twentieth and considers
friendship to be holy.
• Hindu reform movements, such as <color=#3366CC>Ayyavazhi</color>, Swaminarayan Faith and Ananda Marga, are examples of new
religious movements within Indian religions.
• Japanese new religions (shinshukyo) is a general category for a wide variety of religious movements founded in
Japan since the 19th century. These movements share almost nothing in common except the place of their
founding. The largest religious movements centered in Japan include <color=#3366CC>Soka Gakkai</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tenrikyo</color>, and Seicho-No-Ie
among hundreds of smaller groups.
• <color=#3366CC>Jehovah's Witnesses</color>, a <color=#3366CC>non-trinitarian</color> <color=#3366CC>Christian</color> Reformist movement sometimes described as millenarian.
• <color=#3366CC>Neo-Druidism</color> is a religion promoting harmony with nature, named after but not necessarily connected to the Iron
Age <color=#3366CC>druids</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Modern pagan</color> movements attempting to reconstruct or revive ancient <color=#3366CC>pagan</color> practices, such as <color=#3366CC>Heathenry</color>,
Hellenism, Roman Traditionalism, and Kemeticism.
• Noahidism is a monotheistic ideology based on the Seven Laws of Noah, and on their traditional interpretations
within Rabbinic Judaism.
• Some forms of <color=#3366CC>parody religion</color> or fiction-based religion like Jediism, Pastafarianism, Dudeism, "Tolkien religion",
and others often develop their own writings, traditions, and cultural expressions, and end up behaving like
traditional religions.
• <color=#3366CC>Satanism</color> is a broad category of religions that, for example, worship Satan as a deity (Theistic Satanism) or use
Satan as a symbol of carnality and earthly values (<color=#3366CC>LaVeyan Satanism</color> and The Satanic Temple).
• <color=#3366CC>Scientology</color> is characterised by scholarship in psychology and behavioral sciences as a <color=#3366CC>scam</color> or a commercial
business. News sources, politicians and counter-cult organisations have characterised it in similar terms, or as a
<color=#3366CC>cult</color>. Academics who study religious movements classify it as a new religious movement or religion. Its mythological
framework is similar to a <color=#3366CC>UFO cult</color> and includes references to <color=#3366CC>aliens</color>, but it is kept secret from most followers. It
charges a fee for its central activity, on the basis of which it has been characterised as a commercial enterprise.
• <color=#3366CC>UFO Religions</color> in which extraterrestrial entities are an element of belief, such as Raëlism, Aetherius Society, and
Marshall Vian Summers's New Message from God.
• <color=#3366CC>Unitarian Universalism</color> is a religion characterized by support for a free and responsible search for truth and
meaning, and has no accepted <color=#3366CC>creed</color> or <color=#3366CC>theology</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Wicca</color> is a neo-pagan religion first popularised in 1954 by British civil servant <color=#3366CC>Gerald Gardner</color>, involving the worship
of a God and Goddess.
Related aspects
Law
The study of law and religion is a relatively new field, with several thousand scholars involved in law schools, and
academic departments including political science, religion, and history since 1980. Scholars in the field are not only
focused on strictly legal issues about religious freedom or non-establishment, but also study religions as they are
qualified through judicial discourses or legal understanding of religious phenomena. Exponents look at canon law,
natural law, and state law, often in a comparative perspective. Specialists have explored themes in Western history
regarding Christianity and justice and mercy, rule and equity, and discipline and love. Common topics of interest
include marriage and the family and human rights. Outside of Christianity, scholars have looked at law and religion links
in the Muslim Middle East and pagan Rome.
Studies have focused on <color=#3366CC>secularization</color>. In particular, the issue of wearing religious symbols in public, such as
headscarves that are banned in French schools, have received scholarly attention in the context of human rights and
feminism.
Science

<color=#3366CC>Science</color> acknowledges reason and empirical evidence; and religions include <color=#3366CC>revelation</color>, <color=#3366CC>faith</color> and <color=#3366CC>sacredness</color> whilst
also acknowledging philosophical and <color=#3366CC>metaphysical</color> explanations with regard to the study of the universe. Both science
and religion are not monolithic, timeless, or static because both are complex social and cultural endeavors that have
changed through time across languages and cultures.
The concepts of science and religion are a recent invention: the term religion emerged in the 17th century in the midst
of colonization, globalization and the Protestant Reformation. The term science emerged in the 19th century out of
<color=#3366CC>natural philosophy</color> in the midst of attempts to narrowly define those who studied nature (<color=#3366CC>natural science</color>), and the
phrase religion and science emerged in the 19th century due to the reification of both concepts. It was in the 19th
century that the terms Buddhism, Hinduism, Taoism, and Confucianism first emerged. In the ancient and medieval
world, the etymological Latin roots of both science (scientia) and religion (religio) were understood as inner qualities of
the individual or virtues, never as doctrines, practices, or actual sources of knowledge.
In general, the <color=#3366CC>scientific method</color> gains knowledge by testing hypotheses to develop <color=#3366CC>theories</color> through elucidation of facts
or evaluation by <color=#3366CC>experiments</color> and thus only answers <color=#3366CC>cosmological</color> questions about the <color=#3366CC>universe</color> that can be observed
and measured. It develops <color=#3366CC>theories</color> of the world which best fit physically observed evidence. All scientific knowledge is
subject to later refinement, or even rejection, in the face of additional evidence. Scientific theories that have an
overwhelming preponderance of favorable evidence are often treated as de facto verities in general parlance, such as

the theories of <color=#3366CC>general relativity</color> and <color=#3366CC>natural selection</color> to explain respectively the mechanisms of <color=#3366CC>gravity</color> and <color=#3366CC>evolution</color>.
Religion does not have a method per se partly because religions emerge through time from diverse cultures and it is an
attempt to find meaning in the world, and to explain humanity's place in it and relationship to it and to any posited
entities. In terms of Christian theology and ultimate truths, people rely on reason, experience, scripture, and tradition to
test and gauge what they experience and what they should believe. Furthermore, religious models, understanding, and
metaphors are also revisable, as are scientific models.
Regarding religion and science, <color=#3366CC>Albert Einstein</color> states (1940): "For science can only ascertain what is, but not what
should be, and outside of its domain value judgments of all kinds remain necessary. Religion, on the other hand, deals
only with evaluations of human thought and action; it cannot justifiably speak of facts and relationships between
facts...Now, even though the realms of religion and science in themselves are clearly marked off from each other,
nevertheless there exist between the two strong reciprocal relationships and dependencies. Though religion may be
that which determine the goals, it has, nevertheless, learned from science, in the broadest sense, what means will
contribute to the attainment of the goals it has set up."
Morality
Many religions have value frameworks regarding personal behavior meant to guide adherents in determining between
right and wrong. These include the Five Vows of Jainism, Judaism's <color=#3366CC>halakha</color>, Islam's <color=#3366CC>sharia</color>, Catholicism's <color=#3366CC>canon law</color>,
Buddhism's <color=#3366CC>Noble Eightfold Path</color>, and Zoroastrianism's <color=#3366CC>good thoughts, good words, and good deeds</color> concept, among
others.
Religion and morality are not synonymous. While it is often assumed in Christian thought that morality is ultimately
based in religion, it can also have a <color=#3366CC>secular basis</color>.
The study of religion and morality can be contentious due to ethnocentric views on morality, failure to distinguish
between in group and out group altruism, and inconsistent definitions of religiosity.
Politics
Impact
Religion has had a significant impact on the political system in many countries. Notably, most Muslim-majority countries
adopt various aspects of <color=#3366CC>sharia</color>, the Islamic law. Some countries even define themselves in religious terms, such as
<color=#3366CC>The Islamic Republic of Iran</color>. The sharia thus affects up to 23% of the global population, or 1.57 billion people who are
<color=#3366CC>Muslims</color>. However, religion also affects political decisions in many western countries. For instance, in the <color=#3366CC>United States</color>,
51% of voters would be less likely to vote for a presidential candidate who did not believe in God, and only 6% more
likely. Christians made up 92% of members of the US Congress, compared with 71% of the general public (in 2014). At
the same time, while 23% of US adults are religiously unaffiliated, only one former member of Congress (Kyrsten
Sinema, Arizona), or 0.2% of that body, claims no religious affiliation. In most European countries, however, religion
has a much smaller influence on politics although it used to be much more important. For instance, <color=#3366CC>same-sex marriage</color>
and <color=#3366CC>abortion</color> were illegal in many European countries until recently, following Christian (usually <color=#3366CC>Catholic</color>) doctrine.
Several European leaders are atheists (e.g., <color=#3366CC>France</color>'s former president <color=#3366CC>Francois Hollande</color> or Greece's prime minister
Alexis Tsipras). In Asia, the role of religion differs widely between countries. For instance, <color=#3366CC>India</color> is still one of the most
religious countries and religion still has a strong impact on politics, given that Hindu nationalists have been targeting
minorities like the Muslims and the Christians, who historically belonged to the lower castes. By contrast, countries
such as China or Japan are largely secular and thus religion has a much smaller impact on politics.
Secularism
Secularization is the transformation of the politics of a society from close identification with a particular religion's values
and institutions toward nonreligious values and <color=#3366CC>secular</color> institutions. The purpose of this is frequently modernization or
protection of the population's religious diversity.
Economics
One study has found there is a negative correlation between self-defined religiosity and the wealth of nations. In other
words, the richer a nation is, the less likely its inhabitants to call themselves religious, whatever this word means to
them (Many people identify themselves as part of a religion (not irreligion) but do not self-identify as religious).
Sociologist and political economist <color=#3366CC>Max Weber</color> has argued that Protestant Christian countries are wealthier because of
their Protestant work ethic. According to a study from 2015, <color=#3366CC>Christians</color> hold the largest amount of wealth (55% of the
total world wealth), followed by <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color> (5.8%), <color=#3366CC>Hindus</color> (3.3%) and <color=#3366CC>Jews</color> (1.1%). According to the same study it was
found that adherents under the classification <color=#3366CC>Irreligion</color> or other religions hold about 34.8% of the total global wealth
(while making up only about 20% of the world population, see section on classification).
Health
Mayo Clinic researchers examined the association between religious involvement and spirituality, and physical health,
mental health, health-related quality of life, and other health outcomes. The authors reported that: "Most studies have
shown that religious involvement and spirituality are associated with better health outcomes, including greater
longevity, coping skills, and health-related quality of life (even during terminal illness) and less anxiety, depression, and
suicide."
The authors of a subsequent study concluded that the influence of religion on health is largely beneficial, based on a
review of related literature. According to academic James W. Jones, several studies have discovered "positive
correlations between religious belief and practice and mental and physical health and longevity."
An analysis of data from the 1998 US General Social Survey, whilst broadly confirming that religious activity was
associated with better health and well-being, also suggested that the role of different dimensions of
spirituality/religiosity in health is rather more complicated. The results suggested "that it may not be appropriate to
generalize findings about the relationship between spirituality/religiosity and health from one form of
spirituality/religiosity to another, across denominations, or to assume effects are uniform for men and women.
Violence
Critics such as Hector Avalos, Regina Schwartz, <color=#3366CC>Christopher Hitchens</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Richard Dawkins</color> have argued that religions
are inherently violent and harmful to society by using violence to promote their goals, in ways that are endorsed and
exploited by their leaders.
Anthropologist Jack David Eller asserts that religion is not inherently violent, arguing "religion and violence are clearly
compatible, but they are not identical." He asserts that "violence is neither essential to nor exclusive to religion" and
that "virtually every form of religious violence has its nonreligious corollary."
Animal sacrifice
Some (but not all) religions practise <color=#3366CC>animal sacrifice</color>, the <color=#3366CC>ritual</color> killing and offering of an animal to appease or maintain
favour with a <color=#3366CC>deity</color>. It has been banned in <color=#3366CC>India</color>.
Superstition
Greek and Roman pagans, who saw their relations with the gods in political and social terms, scorned the man who
constantly trembled with fear at the thought of the gods (deisidaimonia), as a slave might fear a cruel and capricious
master. The Romans called such fear of the gods superstitio. Ancient Greek historian <color=#3366CC>Polybius</color> described superstition in
<color=#3366CC>ancient Rome</color> as an instrumentum regni, an instrument of maintaining the cohesion of the <color=#3366CC>Empire</color>.
Superstition has been described as the non-rational establishment of cause and effect. Religion is more complex and is
often composed of social institutions and has a moral aspect. Some religions may include superstitions or make use of
magical thinking. Adherents of one religion sometimes think of other religions as superstition. Some <color=#3366CC>atheists</color>, <color=#3366CC>deists</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>skeptics</color> regard religious belief as superstition.
The Roman Catholic Church considers superstition to be sinful in the sense that it denotes a lack of trust in the divine
providence of God and, as such, is a violation of the first of the Ten Commandments. The Catechism of the Catholic
Church states that superstition "in some sense represents a perverse excess of religion" (para. #2110). "Superstition", it
says, "is a deviation of religious feeling and of the practices this feeling imposes. It can even affect the worship we offer
the true God, e.g., when one attributes an importance in some way magical to certain practices otherwise lawful or
necessary. To attribute the efficacy of prayers or of sacramental signs to their mere external performance, apart from
the interior dispositions that they demand is to fall into superstition. Cf. Matthew 23:16–22" (para. #2111)
Agnosticism and atheism
The terms <color=#3366CC>atheist</color> (lack of belief in gods) and agnostic (belief in the unknowability of the existence of gods), though
specifically contrary to theistic (e.g., Christian, Jewish, and Muslim) religious teachings, do not by definition mean the
opposite of religious. The true opposite of religious is the word irreligious. <color=#3366CC>Irreligion</color> describes an absence of any
religion; antireligion describes an active opposition or aversion toward religions in general. There are religions
(including Buddhism and Taoism) that classify some of their followers as agnostic, atheistic, or <color=#3366CC>nontheistic</color>. For
example, in ancient India, there were large atheistic movements and traditions (Nirīśvaravāda) that rejected the <color=#3366CC>Vedas</color>,
such as the atheistic <color=#3366CC>Ājīvika</color> and the Ajñana which taught agnosticism.
Interfaith cooperation
Because religion continues to be recognized in Western thought as a universal impulse, many religious practitioners
have aimed to band together in interfaith dialogue, cooperation, and religious peacebuilding. The first major dialogue
was the <color=#3366CC>Parliament of the World's Religions</color> at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, which affirmed universal values and
recognition of the diversity of practices among different cultures. The 20th century has been especially fruitful in use of
interfaith dialogue as a means of solving ethnic, political, or even religious conflict, with Christian–Jewish reconciliation
representing a complete reverse in the attitudes of many Christian communities towards Jews.
Recent interfaith initiatives include A Common Word, launched in 2007 and focused on bringing Muslim and Christian
leaders together, the "C1 World Dialogue", the Common Ground initiative between Islam and Buddhism, and a <color=#3366CC>United</color>
<color=#3366CC>Nations</color> sponsored "World Interfaith Harmony Week".
Culture
Culture and religion have usually been seen as closely related. <color=#3366CC>Paul Tillich</color> looked at religion as the soul of culture and
culture as the form or framework of religion. In his own words: Religion as ultimate concern is the meaning-giving
substance of culture, and culture is the totality of forms in which the basic concern of religion expresses itself. In
abbreviation: religion is the substance of culture, culture is the form of religion. Such a consideration definitely prevents
the establishment of a dualism of religion and culture. Every religious act, not only in organized religion, but also in the
most intimate movement of the soul, is culturally formed. Ernst Troeltsch, similarly, looked at culture as the soil of
religion and thought that, therefore, transplanting a religion from its original culture to a foreign culture would kill it in the
same manner that transplanting a plant from its natural soil to an alien soil would kill it. However, there have been many
attempts in the modern pluralistic situation to distinguish culture from religion. Domenic Marbaniang has argued that
elements grounded on beliefs of a metaphysical nature (religious) are distinct from elements grounded on nature and
the natural (cultural). For instance, language (with its grammar) is a cultural element while sacralization of language in
which a particular religious scripture is written is more often a religious practice. The same applies to music and the
arts.
Criticism
Criticism of religion is <color=#3366CC>criticism</color> of the ideas, the truth, or the practice of religion, including its political and social
implications.
East Asia

East Asia is a geocultural region of <color=#3366CC>Asia</color>. It includes <color=#3366CC>China</color>, <color=#3366CC>Japan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mongolia</color>, <color=#3366CC>North Korea</color>, <color=#3366CC>South Korea</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Taiwan</color>,

plus two special administrative regions of China: <color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color> and <color=#3366CC>Macau</color>. The economies of <color=#3366CC>China</color>, <color=#3366CC>Japan</color>, <color=#3366CC>South</color>
<color=#3366CC>Korea</color>, and Taiwan are among the world's largest, fastest-growing, and most prosperous. East Asia borders <color=#3366CC>North Asia</color>
to the north, <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color> to the south, <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color> to the southwest, and <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color> to the west. To its east is the
<color=#3366CC>Pacific Ocean</color>.
East Asia, especially the <color=#3366CC>Chinese civilization</color>, is regarded as one of the earliest <color=#3366CC>cradles of civilization</color>. Other ancient
civilizations in East Asia that still exist as independent countries in the present day include the <color=#3366CC>Japanese</color>, <color=#3366CC>Korean</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>Mongolian</color> civilizations. Various other civilizations existed as independent polities in East Asia in the past but have
since been absorbed into neighbouring civilizations in the present day, such as <color=#3366CC>Tibet</color>, <color=#3366CC>Manchuria</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Ryukyu</color>
(<color=#3366CC>Okinawa</color>), among many others. Taiwan has a relatively young <color=#3366CC>history</color> in the region after the prehistoric era; originally, it
was a major site of <color=#3366CC>Austronesian</color> civilization prior to colonization by European colonial powers and China from the 17th
century onward. For thousands of years, China was the leading civilization in the region, exerting influence on its
neighbours. Historically, societies in East Asia have fallen within the <color=#3366CC>Chinese sphere of influence</color>, and East Asian
vocabularies and scripts are often derived from <color=#3366CC>Classical Chinese</color> and <color=#3366CC>Chinese script</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Chinese calendar</color> serves as
the root from which many other East Asian calendars are derived.
Major religions in East Asia include Buddhism (mostly <color=#3366CC>Mahayana</color>), <color=#3366CC>Confucianism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Neo-Confucianism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Taoism</color>,

ancestral worship, and <color=#3366CC>Chinese folk religion</color> in Mainland China, <color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color>, <color=#3366CC>Macau</color> and <color=#3366CC>Taiwan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Shinto</color> in Japan, and

Christianity and <color=#3366CC>Musok</color> in Korea. Tengerism and <color=#3366CC>Tibetan Buddhism</color> are prevalent among <color=#3366CC>Mongols</color> and <color=#3366CC>Tibetans</color> while
other religions such as Shamanism are widespread among the indigenous populations of northeastern China such as

the <color=#3366CC>Manchus</color>. The major languages in East Asia include <color=#3366CC>Mandarin Chinese</color>, <color=#3366CC>Japanese</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Korean</color>. The major ethnic
groups of East Asia include the <color=#3366CC>Han</color> in China and Taiwan, <color=#3366CC>Yamato</color> in Japan, <color=#3366CC>Koreans</color> in North and South Korea, and
<color=#3366CC>Mongols</color> in Mongolia. There are 76 officially-recognized <color=#3366CC>minority</color> or <color=#3366CC>indigenous</color> ethnic groups in East Asia; 55 native to
mainland China (including Hui, Manchus, Chinese Mongols, Tibetans, <color=#3366CC>Uyghurs</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Zhuang</color> in the frontier regions), 16
native to the island of Taiwan (collectively known as <color=#3366CC>Taiwanese indigenous peoples</color>), 1 native to the Japanese island of

<color=#3366CC>Hokkaido</color> (the <color=#3366CC>Ainu</color>) and 4 native to Mongolia (<color=#3366CC>Turkic peoples</color>). The <color=#3366CC>Ryukyuan people</color> are an unrecognized ethnic
group indigenous to the <color=#3366CC>Ryukyu Islands</color> in southern Japan, which stretch from <color=#3366CC>Kyushu</color> to Taiwan. There are also
several unrecognized indigenous ethnic groups in mainland China and Taiwan.
East Asia is inhabited by around 1,648 million people, making up nearly 33% of the population in continental Asia and
20% of the global population. The region is home to major world metropolises such as <color=#3366CC>Beijing</color>–<color=#3366CC>Tianjin</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Busan</color>–<color=#3366CC>Daegu</color>–<color=#3366CC>Ulsan</color>–<color=#3366CC>Changwon</color>, <color=#3366CC>Chongqing</color>, <color=#3366CC>Guangzhou</color>-<color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color>-<color=#3366CC>Macau</color>, <color=#3366CC>Osaka</color>–<color=#3366CC>Kyoto</color>–<color=#3366CC>Kobe</color>, <color=#3366CC>Seoul</color>-<color=#3366CC>Incheon</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Shanghai</color>, <color=#3366CC>Taipei</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Tokyo</color>. Although the coastal and riparian areas of the region form one of the world's most
populated places, the population in <color=#3366CC>Mongolia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Western China</color>, both landlocked areas, is very sparsely distributed,
with Mongolia having the lowest population density of a sovereign state. As of 2025, the overall population density of
the region is 133 PD/km2, about three times the world average of 45 /km2.
History
Ancient era
China was the first region settled in East Asia and was undoubtedly the core of East Asian civilization from where other
parts of East Asia were formed. The various other regions in East Asia were selective in the Chinese influences they
adopted into their local customs. Historian Ping-ti Ho referred to China as the cradle of Eastern civilization, in parallel

with the <color=#3366CC>cradle of Middle Eastern civilization</color> along the <color=#3366CC>Fertile Crescent</color> encompassing <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ancient Egypt</color>
as well as the <color=#3366CC>cradle of Western civilization</color> encompassing <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greece</color>.
Chinese civilization emerged early, and prefigured other East Asian civilisations. Throughout history, imperial China
would exert cultural, economic, technological, and political influence on its neighbours. Succeeding Chinese dynasties
exerted enormous influence across East Asia culturally, economically, politically and militarily for over two millennia.
The <color=#3366CC>tributary system of China</color> shaped much of East Asia's history for over two millennia due to Imperial China's
economic and cultural influence over the region, and thus played a huge role in the history of East Asia in particular.
Imperial China's cultural preeminence not only led the country to become East Asia's first literate nation in the entire
region, it also supplied Japan and Korea with Chinese loanwords and linguistic influences rooted in their writing
systems.
Under <color=#3366CC>Emperor Wu of Han</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Han dynasty</color> made China the regional powerhouse in East Asia, projecting much of its
imperial influence onto its neighbours. Han China hosted the largest unified population in East Asia, the most literate
and urbanised as well as being the most economically developed, as well as the most technologically and culturally
advanced civilization in the region at the time. Cultural and religious interaction between the Chinese and other regional
East Asian dynasties and kingdoms occurred. China's impact and influence on Korea began with the Han dynasty's
northeastern expansion in 108 BC when the Han Chinese conquered the northern part of the Korean peninsula and
established a province called Lelang. Chinese influences were transmitted and soon took root in Korea through the
inclusion of the Chinese writing system, monetary system, rice culture, philosophical schools of thought, and Confucian
political institutions. Jomon society in ancient Japan incorporated wet-rice cultivation and metallurgy through its contact
with Korea. Starting in the fourth century AD, Japan adopted <color=#3366CC>Chinese characters</color>, which remain integral to the
<color=#3366CC>Japanese writing system</color>. Utilizing the Chinese writing system allowed the Japanese to conduct their daily activities,
maintain historical records and give form to various ideas, thoughts, and philosophies.
Medieval era
During the <color=#3366CC>Tang dynasty</color>, China exerted its greatest influence on East Asia as various aspects of <color=#3366CC>Chinese culture</color>
spread to Japan and Korea. The establishment of the medieval Tang dynasty rekindled the impetus of Chinese
expansionism across the geopolitical confines of East Asia. Similar to its <color=#3366CC>Han</color> predecessor, Tang China reasserted
itself as the center of East Asian geopolitical influence during the early medieval period which spearheaded and
marked another golden age in Chinese history. In addition, Tang China also managed to maintain control over northern
Vietnam and <color=#3366CC>northern Korea</color>.
As full-fledged medieval East Asian states were established, Korea by the fourth century AD and Japan by the seventh
century AD, Japan and Korea actively began to incorporate Chinese influences such as <color=#3366CC>Confucianism</color>, the use of

<color=#3366CC>Chinese characters</color>, <color=#3366CC>architecture</color>, state institutions, <color=#3366CC>political philosophies</color>, religion, urban planning, and various <color=#3366CC>scientific</color>
<color=#3366CC>and technological</color> methods into their culture and society through direct contacts with Tang China and succeeding
Chinese dynasties. Drawing inspiration from the Tang political system, Prince Naka no Ōe launched the <color=#3366CC>Taika Reform</color>
in 645 AD where he radically transformed Japan's political bureaucracy into a more centralized bureaucratic empire.
The Japanese also adopted <color=#3366CC>Mahayana</color> Buddhism, Chinese style architecture, and the imperial court's rituals and
ceremonies, including the orchestral music and state dances had Tang influences. Written Chinese gained prestige and
aspects of Tang culture such as <color=#3366CC>poetry</color>, <color=#3366CC>calligraphy</color>, and <color=#3366CC>landscape painting</color> became widespread. During the Nara
period, Japan began to aggressively import Chinese culture and styles of government which included Confucian
protocol that served as a foundation for Japanese culture as well as political and social philosophy. The Japanese
created laws adopted from the Chinese legal system that was used to govern in addition to the <color=#3366CC>kimono</color>, which was
inspired from Chinese <color=#3366CC>hanfu</color> during the 8th century.
Modern era
For many centuries, most notably from the 7th to the 14th centuries, China stood as East Asia's most advanced
civilization and foremost military and economic power, exerting its influence as the transmission of advanced Chinese
cultural practices and ways of thinking greatly shaped the region up until the 19th century. From the 3rd century
through the 18th century, diplomatic and trade relations between China and other East Asian countries and the steppe
kingdoms was governed through a tributary system. Under this system, the Chinese emperor received tribute from
other rulers and in return received political benefits (like recognition or non-aggression agreements) or physical gifts,
like porcelain and silks. Through this system, the Chinese emperor conferred legitimacy on other rulers.
As East Asia's connections with Europe and the Western world strengthened during the late 19th century, China's
power began to decline. By the mid-19th century, the weakening <color=#3366CC>Qing dynasty</color> became fraught with political corruption,
obstacles and stagnation that was incapable of rejuvenating itself as a world power in contrast to the industrializing
Imperial European colonial powers and a rapidly modernizing Japan. The United States Commodore <color=#3366CC>Matthew C. Perry</color>
would <color=#3366CC>open Japan to Western influence</color>, and the country would expand in earnest after the 1860s. Around the same
time, the <color=#3366CC>Meiji Restoration</color> in Japan sparked rapid societal transformation from an isolated feudal state into East Asia's
first industrialised nation. The modern and militarily powerful Japan would galvanise its position in the Orient as East
Asia's greatest power with a global mission poised to advance to lead the entire world. By the early 1900s, the <color=#3366CC>Empire</color>
<color=#3366CC>of Japan</color> succeeded in asserting itself as East Asia's most dominant geopolitical force.
With its newly found international status, Japan began to challenge the European colonial powers and took on a more
active role within the East Asian geopolitical order and world affairs at large. Flexing its political and military might,
Japan soundly defeated the Qing dynasty during the <color=#3366CC>First Sino-Japanese War</color> as well as defeating Russia in the
<color=#3366CC>Russo-Japanese War</color> in 1905; the first major military victory in the modern era of an East Asian power over a European
one.
During <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>, European military presence in East Asia decreased. Japan viewed this as an opportunity to
increase its power in China and shortly after the war began, occupied Germany's concessions in <color=#3366CC>Shandong</color>. In
December 1914, Japan made its Twenty-One Demands to China. The <color=#3366CC>Republic of China</color> under <color=#3366CC>Yuan Shikai</color> conceded
to most of the demands in 1915, and subsequent treaties and agreements further increased Japan's semi-colonial
power in China.
Japan hegemony was the heart of an empire that would include <color=#3366CC>Taiwan</color> and <color=#3366CC>Korea</color>. During <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>, Japanese
expansionism with its imperialist aspirations through the <color=#3366CC>Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere</color> would incorporate
Korea, Taiwan, much of eastern China and Manchuria, Hong Kong, and Southeast Asia under its control establishing
itself as a maritime colonial power in East Asia.
Contemporary era
After a century of exploitation by the European and Japanese colonialists, post-colonial East Asia saw the <color=#3366CC>defeat</color> and
<color=#3366CC>occupation of Japan</color> by the victorious Allies. The end of World War II did not result in east Asian countries obtaining
independence or national unification. Independence and national unification were primary concerns for the first
generation of east Asian post-World War II leaders.
The <color=#3366CC>Chinese Civil War</color> resumed after the defeat of the Japanese, with the Communists defeating the Nationalist
Republic of China government. The <color=#3366CC>government of the Republic of China retreated to Taiwan</color> and the People's
Republic of China was proclaimed on 1 October 1949.
Post-war, the Korean peninsula was partitioned, leading to the development of the Democratic People's Republic of
Korea (<color=#3366CC>North Korea</color>) and the Republic of Korea (<color=#3366CC>South Korea</color>). The <color=#3366CC>Korean War</color> (1950–1953) increased regional and
international tensions. The northeast part of East Asia hardened along communist and anti-communist lines. South
Korea, Taiwan, and the United States have increased their ties.
During the latter half of the 20th century, the region would see the <color=#3366CC>post war economic miracle of Japan</color>, which ushered
in three decades of unprecedented growth, only to experience an <color=#3366CC>economic slowdown during the 1990s</color>, but
nonetheless Japan continues to remain a global economic power. East Asia would also see the economic rise of Hong
Kong, <color=#3366CC>South Korea</color>, and Taiwan, in addition to the respective handovers of <color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color> and Macau near the end of the
20th century.
The onset of the 21st century in East Asia led to the integration of <color=#3366CC>China into the global economy</color> through its entry in
the World Trade Organization while also enhancing its emerging international status as a potential world power
reinforced with its aim of restoring its historical established significance and enduring international prominence in the
world economy.
As of at least 2022, the region is more peaceful, integrated, wealthy, and stable than at any time in the previous 150
years.
Definitions
In common usage, the term "East Asia" typically refers to a region including <color=#3366CC>Greater China</color>, <color=#3366CC>Japan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Korea</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Mongolia</color>.
<color=#3366CC>China</color>, Japan, and Korea represent the three core countries and civilizations of traditional East Asia, as they once had
a shared written language, a shared culture, and a shared Confucian societal value system (involving shared Confucian
philosophical tenets) once instituted by Imperial China. Other usages define China, Japan, North Korea, South Korea
and Taiwan as countries that constitute East Asia based on their geographic proximity as well as historical and modern
cultural and economic ties, particularly with Japan and Korea in having retained strong cultural influences that
originated from China. Some scholars include <color=#3366CC>Vietnam</color> as part of East Asia as it has been considered part of the
greater <color=#3366CC>Chinese cultural sphere</color>. Though Confucianism continues to play an important role in Vietnamese culture,
Chinese characters are no longer used in its written language and many scholarly organizations classify Vietnam as a
Southeast Asian country. Mongolia is geographically north of China yet Confucianism and the Chinese writing system
and culture had limited impact on Mongolian society. Thus, Mongolia is sometimes grouped with Central Asian

countries such as <color=#3366CC>Turkmenistan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kyrgyzstan</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Kazakhstan</color>. <color=#3366CC>Xinjiang</color> and <color=#3366CC>Tibet</color> are sometimes seen as part of
Central Asia (see also Greater Central Asia).
Broader and looser definitions by international agencies and organisations such as the <color=#3366CC>World Bank</color> refer to East Asia
as the "three major Northeast Asian economies, i.e. China, Japan, and South Korea", as well as Mongolia, North
Korea, the <color=#3366CC>Russian Far East</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Siberia</color>. The Council on Foreign Relations includes the Russia Far East, Mongolia,
and <color=#3366CC>Nepal</color>. The World Bank also acknowledges the roles of Chinese special administrative regions <color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Macau</color>, as well as <color=#3366CC>Taiwan</color>, a country with limited recognition. The Economic Research Institute for Northeast Asia
defines the region as "China, Japan, the Koreas, Nepal, Mongolia, and eastern regions of the <color=#3366CC>Russian Federation</color>".
The UNSD definition of East Asia is based on statistical convenience, but others commonly use the same definition of
China, Hong Kong, Macau, Mongolia, North Korea, South Korea, Taiwan, and Japan.
Certain Japanese islands are associated with Oceania due to non-continental geology, distance from mainland Asia or
biogeographical similarities with <color=#3366CC>Micronesia</color>. Some groups, such as the <color=#3366CC>World Health Organization</color>, categorize China,
Japan and Korea with Australia and the rest of Oceania. The World Health Organization label this region the "Western
Pacific", with East Asia not being used in their concept of major world regions. Their definition of this region further
includes Mongolia and the adjacent area of <color=#3366CC>Cambodia</color>, as well as the countries of the Southeast Asia Archipelago
(excluding <color=#3366CC>East Timor</color>, <color=#3366CC>Thailand</color>, <color=#3366CC>Myanmar</color> and <color=#3366CC>Indonesia</color>).
Alternative definitions
In the context of business and economics, "East Asia" is sometimes used to refer to the geographical area covering ten

<color=#3366CC>Southeast Asian</color> countries in <color=#3366CC>ASEAN</color>, <color=#3366CC>Greater China</color>, Japan, and Korea. However, in this context, the term "<color=#3366CC>Far East</color>" is
used by the Europeans to cover ASEAN countries and the countries in East Asia. On rare occasions, the term is also
sometimes taken to include <color=#3366CC>India</color> and other South Asian countries that are not situated within the bounds of the
Asia-Pacific, although the term Indo-Pacific is more commonly used for such a definition.
Observers preferring a broader definition of "East Asia" often use the term <color=#3366CC>Northeast Asia</color> to refer to China, the Korean
Peninsula, and Japan, with the region of <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color> covering the ten <color=#3366CC>ASEAN</color> countries. This usage, which is seen
in economic and diplomatic discussions, is at odds with the historical meanings of both "East Asia" and "Northeast
Asia". The Council on Foreign Relations of the United States defines Northeast Asia as Japan and Korea.
Climate
East Asia is home to many climatic zones. It also has unique weather patterns such as the East Asian rainy season
and the <color=#3366CC>East Asian Monsoon</color>.
Climate change
Like the rest of the world, East Asia has been getting warmer due to climate change, and there had been a measurable
increase in the frequency and severity of <color=#3366CC>heatwaves</color>. The region is also expected to see the intensification of its
monsoon, leading to more flooding. China has notably embarked on the sponge cities program, where cities are
designed to increase the area of urban green spaces and permeable pavings in order to help deal with <color=#3366CC>flash floods</color>
caused by greater precipitation extremes. Under high-warming scenarios, "critical health thresholds" for heat stress
during the 21st century will be at times breached, in areas like the <color=#3366CC>North China Plain</color>.
China, Japan and the Republic of Korea are expected to see some of the largest economic losses caused by sea level
rise. The city of <color=#3366CC>Guangzhou</color> is projected to experience the single largest annual economic losses from sea level rise in
the world, potentially reaching US$254 million by 2050. Under the highest climate change scenario and in the absence
of adaptation, cumulative economic losses caused by sea level rise in Guangzhou would exceed US$1 trillion by 2100.
<color=#3366CC>Shanghai</color> is also expected to experience annual losses of around 1% of the local GDP in the absence of adaptation.
The <color=#3366CC>Yangtze River</color> basin is a sensitive and biodiverse ecosystem, yet around 20% of its species may be lost
throughout the century under 2 C-change and ~43% under 4.5 C-change.

Culture
The culture of East Asia, has been <color=#3366CC>deeply influenced by China</color>, as it was the civilization that had the most dominant
influence in the region throughout the ages that ultimately laid the foundation for East Asian civilization. The vast
knowledge and ingenuity of Chinese civilization and the classics of Chinese literature and culture were seen as the
foundations for a civilized life in East Asia. <color=#3366CC>Imperial China</color> served as a vehicle through which the adoption of Confucian
ethical philosophy, Chinese calendar system, political and legal systems, architectural style, diet, terminology,
institutions, religious beliefs, <color=#3366CC>imperial examinations</color> that emphasised a knowledge of Chinese classics, political
philosophy and cultural value systems, as well as historically sharing a common writing system reflected in the histories
of <color=#3366CC>Japan</color> and <color=#3366CC>Korea</color>.
The Imperial Chinese tributary system was the bedrock of network of trade and foreign relations between China and its
East Asian tributaries, which helped to shape much of East Asian affairs during the ancient and medieval eras. Through
the tributary system, the various dynasties of Imperial China facilitated frequent economic and cultural exchange that
influenced the cultures of Japan and Korea and drew them into a Chinese international order. The Imperial Chinese
tributary system shaped much of East Asia's foreign policy and trade for over two millennia due to Imperial China's
economic and cultural dominance over the region, and thus played a huge role in the history of East Asia in particular.
The relationship between China and its cultural influence on East Asia has been compared to the historical influence of
Greco-Roman civilization on classical Western civilisation.
Since the late 19th century, the initially unequal encounter with <color=#3366CC>Western influences</color> has also shaped East Asia,
primarily in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan.
Festivals
• Japan switched the date to the <color=#3366CC>Gregorian calendar</color> after the Meiji Restoration.
Entertainment
East Asian popular culture, such as <color=#3366CC>anime</color> and <color=#3366CC>manga</color> from Japan and <color=#3366CC>K-pop</color> and K-dramas from South Korea, have
become highly popular worldwide in the 21st century.
Sports
<color=#3366CC>Baseball</color> is one of the main sports in East Asia, having been introduced through mid-19th century American contact
and further spread by the Japanese Empire. The game has gained millions of fans in China since the 2010s.
In 1964, Japan was the first Asian nation to hold the <color=#3366CC>Olympic Games</color> after two unsuccessful 1940 attempts in Sapporo
and Tokyo were cancelled due to World War II. 2002 saw Japan and South Korea host the <color=#3366CC>FIFA World Cup</color>, marking
the first time two nations served as hosts of the competition together, as well as the first World Cup in Asia. Between
2018 and 2022, three Olympic Games were held in the region: Pyeongchang hosted the Winter Games in 2018, Tokyo
held the Summer Games in 2021, and Beijing became the first city to host both Summer and Winter Olympics after
hosting the Winter Games in 2022, having run the Summer Games in 2008. The Tokyo 2020 and Beijing 2022 events
were significantly scaled back due to the COVID-19 pandemic, with the Tokyo Games being postponed until 2021.
East Asian Youth Games
Following the discontinuation of the East Asian Games after the 2013 edition, the East Asian Youth Games were
established as their successor. Organized by the East Asian Games Association (EAGA) they are held every four years
among athletes from East Asian countries and territories of the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA), as well as <color=#3366CC>Guam</color>, a
member of the Oceania National Olympic Committees. Although the inaugural edition was originally scheduled for
<color=#3366CC>Taichung</color>, Taiwan, in 2019, it was cancelled; the first edition to be held took place in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, in 2023.
It is one of five Regional Games of the OCA. The others are the Central Asian Games, the Southeast Asian Games
(SEA Games), the South Asian Games, and the West Asian Games.
